§ 2Content

§ 3PREAMBLE

  • It is an introductory statement in a Constitution, which states the reasons and guiding values of the Constitution.
  • It contains the summary or the essence of the Constitution.
  • Tells us about the philosophy of the Constitution.
  • It was made after the entire Constitution was compiled.
  • It is a modified version of the Objective Resolution presented by J.L. Nehru before the Constituent Assembly.
  • Presented on: Dec 13, 1946
  • Adopted on: Jan 22, 1947

Comments on Preamble

  • ID Card of Constitution: N. A. Palkhivala
  • Political Horoscope of Constitution: K. M. Munshi
  • Jewel set: Pt. Thakur Das

Understanding the Preamble

  • Source of power of Constitution
  • → "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA......"
  • This shows that the constitution has been drawn up and enacted by the people through their representatives, and not handed down to them by a king or any outside powers.
THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA PREAMBLE — WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a (SOVEREIGN, SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC) and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the (unity and integrity of the Nation); IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

Nature of the Constitution

#### SOVEREIGN

  • People have supreme right to make decisions on internal as well as external matters. No external power can dictate the government of India.

#### SOCIALIST

  • Wealth is generated socially and should be shared equally by society.
  • Government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities.
  • Example: Russia
  • → Capitalistic: USA
  • → Mixed: India

#### SECULAR

  • Citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion or no religion at all. There is no official state religion. Government treats all religious beliefs and practices equally and impartially.
  • In India, secularism follows a positive concept. (Involvement of state in religious matters)

#### DEMOCRATIC

  • The government functions according to a set of constitutional rules and principles.
  • A Government Of the People, By the People, For the People

#### REPUBLIC

  • A system of government in which the head of the state is elected by the people and not based on a hereditary succession.
  • UK is not a Republic State.

Objectives of the Constitution

#### JUSTICE

  • Citizens cannot be discriminated on the grounds of caste, religion, and gender. Social inequalities have to be reduced.
  • Three types of justice are given in Preamble: Social, Economic and Political

#### LIBERTY

  • There are no unreasonable restrictions on a citizen in what they think, how they wish to express their thoughts and the way they wish to follow up their thoughts in action.
  • Five forms of liberty are given in Preamble: Thought, Expression, Belief, Faith, and Worship

#### EQUALITY

  • All are equal before the law. The traditional social inequalities must end. The government should ensure equal opportunities for all.
  • Two types of equality are given in Preamble: Status and Opportunity

#### FRATERNITY

  • All of us should behave as if we are members of the same family. No one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.
The terms "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity and Republic" are taken from France and the Ideals of Justice are taken from Russia.

Is Preamble a Part of Constitution and is it Amendable?

Berubari Union Case: 1960

  • Supreme Court held that—
  • i) The Preamble is not a part of the Constitution & hence cannot be amended.
  • ii) It is just a key to understanding the Constitution.
  • iii) is not legally enforceable.

Kesavananda Bharati Case: 1973

  • In this case, Supreme Court Overruled the Berubari view and held that
  • i) The Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
  • ii) It reflects the basic structure of the Constitution

LIC of India Case: 1995

  • i) Reaffirmed the Kesavananda Bharati case ruling.
Preamble has been amended only once in 1976 through 42nd Constitutional Amendment. It added the terms: Integrity, Socialist, Secular (TRICK: ISS/SIS)

Enforceability of Preamble

  • It is not enforceable in the Court of Law.
  • It is neither a source of Power nor Restriction to the legislature, but it can be considered as an aid to the legal interpretation of the Constitution.

§ 4SALIENT FEATURES OF THE CONSTITUTION

  • Indian Constitution is the lengthiest written Constitution in the world.
  • Originally Constitution contained: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules
  • Presently it contains: 448 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules
  • Part 7 has been deleted and new Parts: IV-A, IX-A, IX-B, and XIV-A have been added.

Written vs Unwritten Constitution

Written ConstitutionUnwritten Constitution
Compiled and structured in a systematic form.Not structured
Formally constitutedNot formally constituted
Not easy to amendEasy to amend
Ex: IndiaEx: UK

§ 5FEDERALISM

  • This refers to the existence of more than one level of government in the country.
  • Three tier government exists in India:
  • Union/Centre
  • States
  • Local Bodies
  • Under federalism, the states are not merely agents of federal government, they derive their authority from Constitution itself.
India has a: Federation with a unitary bias. Federation with a strong Centre.

Federal features vs Unitary features

Federal FeaturesUnitary Features
Written ConstitutionSingle Constitution
Supremacy of the ConstitutionSingle Citizenship
Rigidity of ConstitutionIntegrated Judiciary
Independence of JudiciaryAll India Services
BicameralismEmergency provisions
Dual GovernmentAppointment of governors by centre

Comments on Indian Federalism

  • Quasi Federal: By K. C. Wheare
  • Cooperative Federalism: By Granville Austin
  • Bargaining Federalism: By Morris Jones
  • Federalism with centralising tendency: By Ivor Jennings

India has a Parliamentary form of Government, having—

3 organs of government:

  • LEGISLATIVE - makes laws
  • EXECUTIVE - carries out laws
  • JUDICIAL - evaluates laws

§ 6SCHEDULES OF INDIAN CONSTITUTION

  • Schedule 1: Names of States and UTs and their territorial jurisdiction
  • Schedule 2: Provisions relating to emoluments and allowances.
  • President, VP, Governor, Speaker + Deputy Speaker (LS+LA), Chairman + Deputy Chairman (RS + LC), Judges (SC + HC), CAG
  • Schedule 3: Oaths and affirmations (Union + State) Ministers, MPs, MLAs, Judges, CAG
  • Schedule 4: Allocation of seats in Rajya Sabha.
  • Schedule 5: Provisions relating to administration of scheduled areas and scheduled tribes.
  • Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana
  • Schedule 6: Provisions related to administration of tribal areas.
  • Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya, Mizoram
  • TRICK: ATM without Money (Manipur is not included)
  • Schedule 7: 3 lists containing subject in which Union and States can make laws. (Federal Provisions)
  • Union list, State list, Concurrent list
  • Union List Subjects: Initially 97, presently 100 subjects (Defence, arms and ammunition, atomic energy, citizenship, airways, inter-state trade and commerce, banking, foreign affairs, labour and mines, census, etc.)
  • State List Subjects: Initially 66, presently 61 subjects. (Public order, local government, health, pilgrimage, liquor, agriculture, fisheries, betting and gambling, etc.)
  • Concurrent List Subjects: Initially 47, presently 52 subjects. Both State and Centre can make laws about subjects given in this list. (Marriage and divorce, insolvency and bankruptcy, trade and labour disputes, electricity, education, weights and measure, etc.)
  • Residuary List:
  • These subjects are not included in Union/State/Concurrent list
  • Parliament has the power to legislate on residuary subjects.
  • Subjects Transferred through 42nd Amendment (State list to Concurrent list):
  • Education
  • Forests
  • Weights and Measures
  • Protection of wild animals and birds
  • Administration of justice
  • Amendment: a formal change to law, contract, constitution, or other legal document.
  • Schedule 8: Official languages
  • Originally there were 14 languages.
  • Presently there are 22 languages.

Here's a list of constitutional amendments that added following languages in the list:

  • 21st CAA, 1967 → Sindhi was added.
  • 71st CAA, 1992 → Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali (Trick: KMN)
  • 92nd CAA, 2003 → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (Trick: BDSM)
  • 96th CAA, 2011 → It changed the name 'Oriya' to 'Odia'

  • Schedule 9: Provisions related to land reforms and Zamindari system. (Added through 1st CA: 1951)
  • Schedule 10: Provisions relating to disqualification of MPs and MLAs on grounds of defection. (52nd CA: 1985)
  • Schedule 11: Provisions relating to Panchayat. 73rd CA: 1992, 29 functional matters
  • Schedule 12: Provisions relating to Municipalities. 74th CA: 1992, 18 functional matters
  • *CA, here, refers to Constitutional Amendment
